SECTION 010:00–6:17

The entry rule and the shapes

The familiar dot-product rule is the first of five views.

Strang begins by making the rules of matrix multiplication explicit. Write C = AB. The entry cij comes from row i of A and column j of B: multiply corresponding entries and add.

The lecture uses c34 as a concrete index example:

c₃₄ = a₃₁b₁₄ + a₃₂b₂₄ + ··· + a₃ₙbₙ₄.

In general,

cij=∑k=1naikbkj

The index k moves across the row of A and down the column of B. Those two vectors must have the same length. If A is m × n and B is n × p, multiplication is defined and C has shape m × p.

Check the dimensions first

(m × n)(n × p) gives m × p. The two inner dimensions must match.

This entry-by-entry calculation is familiar, but the lecture’s central point is that the same product can be understood in several larger pieces.

SECTION 026:17–10:04

Build the product one column at a time

Each column of C is A times the corresponding column of B.

Think of B as a collection of p columns sitting side by side. Multiply A by its first column to get the first column of C. Multiply A by its second column to get the second column of C, and continue.

B = [ b₁   b₂   ···   bₚ ]
AB = [ Ab₁   Ab₂   ···   Abₚ ].

This uses the matrix–vector product from Lecture 1. Multiplying A by a vector makes a linear combination of the columns of A. Therefore every column of C is a combination of the columns of A.

Which combination? Column j of B provides the coefficients for column j of C. The other columns of B do not enter that particular output column.

The shapes support this interpretation: columns of both A and C have m entries, while each coefficient vector from B has n entries, one for each column of A.

SECTION 0310:04–11:39

Build the product one row at a time

The output rows are combinations of the rows of B.

There is a parallel row interpretation. Take row i of A and multiply it by B. That produces row i of C.

row i of C = (row i of A) B.

A row vector multiplying B takes a combination of B’s rows. Thus row i of C is ai1 times row 1 of B, plus ai2 times row 2 of B, and so on.

Keep the two statements straight: columns of the answer come from columns of A; rows of the answer come from rows of B. The intervening matrix supplies the coefficients.

These are not different definitions of multiplication. They organize the same entry products into whole columns or whole rows.

SECTION 0411:39–15:06

A column times a row gives a matrix

Reverse the small shapes and the output becomes full-sized.

A row times a column gives a single number. What happens in the opposite order, a column times a row? The dimensions are (m × 1)(1 × p), so the output is an entire m × p matrix.

Strang uses the example

[234][16]=[212318424]

Each output row is a multiple of (1, 6): the multipliers are 2, 3, and 4. Each output column is a multiple of (2, 3, 4)T: the multipliers are 1 and 6.

This is therefore a very special matrix. The multiplication creates a full-sized rectangle of entries, but all its columns have the same direction, and all its rows have the same direction.

SECTION 0515:06–18:18

Add column–row products to obtain AB

Pair column k of A with row k of B, then sum.

The fourth view of multiplication pairs each column of A with the corresponding row of B. Every pair produces an m × p matrix, so those matrices can be added:

AB = ∑ₖ (column k of A)(row k of B).

For the lecture’s example,

[273849][1600]=[212318424]

The first term is the column (2, 3, 4)T times the row (1, 6), which we just calculated. The second term is the column (7, 8, 9)T times the zero row (0, 0), so it contributes the zero matrix.

Strang then describes the resulting matrix’s row space and column space. All combinations of its rows stay on the line through (1, 6). All combinations of its columns stay on the line through (2, 3, 4)T. Both spaces are lines, even though the matrix has six entries.

SECTION 0618:18–21:22

Multiply compatible blocks

The same rule works when the entries are submatrices.

The fifth view cuts the matrices into blocks. For example, divide each square matrix into four square blocks, as Strang does on the board:

A = [ A₁   A₂ ;   A₃   A₄ ]
B = [ B₁   B₂ ;   B₃   B₄ ].

The top-left block of AB is A₁B₁ + A₂B₃: the first block row of A times the first block column of B. The factors are themselves matrices, so their dimensions must match and their order matters.

Completing the same rule gives the other blocks: A₁B₂ + A₂B₄ at top right, A₃B₁ + A₄B₃ at bottom left, and A₃B₂ + A₄B₄ at bottom right.

The lecture suggests two 20 × 20 matrices partitioned into 10 × 10 blocks as an easy size example. Equal-sized square blocks are convenient, but the essential condition is compatible block dimensions.

Completed pattern. The top-left formula is explicitly developed in the lecture. The other three formulas here are editorial expansions of that same block rule.

All five views—entries, columns, rows, column–row products, and blocks—perform the same underlying scalar multiplications.

SECTION 0721:22–24:14

What an inverse means

For a square matrix, multiplication by the inverse produces I.

Now turn to square matrices. A may or may not have an inverse. If it does, the inverse A−1 satisfies

A⁻¹A = I   and   AA⁻¹ = I.

The identity matrix leaves every vector unchanged. Thus applying A and then A−1 returns the original vector. The two matrices undo each other.

For square matrices, a left inverse is also a right inverse. Strang emphasizes that this fact is not immediate, even though the dimensions allow both products. For rectangular matrices the situation can differ; this lecture concentrates on square matrices.

A square matrix with an inverse is called invertible or nonsingular. The next two sections investigate a matrix for which an inverse cannot exist.

SECTION 0824:14–27:34

Why columns on one line prevent an inverse

The product cannot manufacture directions missing from A.

Strang’s singular example is

A=[1326]

The second column is three times the first. Therefore every combination of its columns lies on the line through (1, 2)T.

Suppose some matrix B could satisfy AB = I. The column rule says that every column of AB must be a combination of A’s columns. In particular, the first column of AB would have to stay on that one line.

But the first column of I is (1, 0)T, which is not on the line. There is no choice of B that makes AB equal to I. This is a geometric reason the inverse cannot exist.

Strang also notes that the determinant is zero. The column argument gives the failure a picture: multiplication cannot produce the independent directions required by the identity.

SECTION 0927:34–31:52

A nonzero vector sent to zero

A contradiction that rules out an inverse.

A second reason is even more useful. For the same matrix, a nonzero vector is taken to zero:

[1326][3−1]=[00]

The first entry is 3 − 3 = 0, and the second is 6 − 6 = 0. The coefficients 3 and −1 give a nontrivial combination of the columns that cancels completely.

Why does that prevent an inverse? Assume an inverse exists and multiply Ax = 0 on the left by A−1:

x = (A⁻¹A)x = A⁻¹0 = 0.

This contradicts x = (3, −1)T, which is not zero. Once multiplication by A has sent this nonzero vector to zero, another matrix cannot recover it by multiplying zero.

The crucial condition

Finding a nonzero x with Ax = 0 rules out an inverse. The zero vector itself proves nothing, because A0 = 0 for every matrix.

SECTION 1031:52–36:39

Find the inverse one column at a time

The identity supplies the right-hand sides.

Return to a matrix that does have an inverse:

A=[1327]

The two columns now point in different directions. To find A−1, start with four unknown entries:

[1327][acbd]=[1001]

Read this product by columns. The first inverse column (a, b)T must solve A(a, b)T = (1, 0)T. The second inverse column (c, d)T must solve A(c, d)T = (0, 1)T.

Finding the inverse is therefore solving two systems with the same coefficient matrix and different right-hand sides. In general, column j of A−1 solves Ax = column j of I.

Gauss–Jordan elimination solves these systems together by carrying both right-hand sides through the same row operations.

SECTION 1136:39–42:43

Gauss–Jordan: reduce [A | I]

Eliminate downward and upward to turn A into I.

Append the two columns of I to A, producing the augmented matrix [A | I]. Apply every row operation to the entire augmented row, including both right-hand sides.

1. Clear the entry below the first pivot

Subtract twice row 1 from row 2:

R₂ ← R₂ − 2R₁.

The left block becomes (1, 3; 0, 1). On the right, the second row changes from (0, 1) to (−2, 1). Ordinary forward elimination has reached an upper triangular matrix.

2. Continue upward

Use the second pivot to clear the 3 above it:

R₁ ← R₁ − 3R₂.

On the right, the first row becomes (1, 0) − 3(−2, 1) = (7, −3). The left block is now I. The right block is

A−1=[7−3−21]

3. Check the result

Multiply the proposed inverse by A. The four entries are 7 − 6 = 1; 21 − 21 = 0; −2 + 2 = 0; and −6 + 7 = 1. The result is I.

SECTION 1242:43–46:34

Why the other block becomes A⁻¹

The same elimination matrix acts on both halves.

The mechanics work, but why must the right-hand block be the inverse? Strang answers using the elimination matrices from Lecture 2.

Each row operation is left multiplication by an elementary matrix. Combine all of them, in their original order, into a single matrix E. Since the entire augmented matrix undergoes the same operations,

E[A | I] = [EA | EI].

The left block was reduced to I, so EA = I. For this square matrix, that identifies E as A−1. On the right, EI is simply E, and therefore equals A−1.

For this particular calculation, the two operation matrices are

[1−301][10−21]=[7−3−21]

The matrix on the right of the product acts first: it subtracts twice row 1 from row 2. The next matrix subtracts three times the updated row 2 from row 1. Their product is exactly the inverse found by augmentation.

Worked expansion. The proof EA = I ⇒ E = A−1 is Strang’s board argument. The explicit two-matrix product is an editorial calculation using his two row operations.

The general procedure is the same: solve n systems together by appending the n columns of the identity. If elimination turns the left half into I, the right half contains the n columns of A−1.
